# Entry contract

Entry contract: v16, 2026-09-21.

Open your first reply of every session with the `Entry contract:` line above, verbatim.

<straw-dog until="01-0020 is done" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0020-pacer.md">
Run /recall first in every session, whatever the first message says.
</straw-dog>

## General rules

A **shape** is whatever is under consideration, held between an idea and a thing: formed enough
to have a context and a structure, not yet exhausted by any one realization. Being a shape says
nothing about being load-bearing — an implementation method is a shape too. → [glossary](.agents/glossary.md).

- Do not generalize from one shape. Preserve a seam. Generalize only when a second materially different shape forces the same concept.
- Explore shape context - what is the shape one of? what are its relationships? does its scope overlap any other shape?
- Explore shape structure - how this shape is/can be built? does expanding its structure change the contract or even what the shape is?

- Changing how the work is done — a skill, a check, a record, the loop — is mechanism work: use [/mechanism](.agents/skills/mechanism/SKILL.md). Building what the project produces is not.

- An `<installed>` block in a file is not that file's to edit. Change the rule in the rules file of the mechanism named on the block, and re-install.

- Recency for evidence, longevity for principles.

- Clarity and simplicity first — Occam's razor: take the shape with the fewest parts that does the job, and remove before you add.

<straw-dog until="01-0018 declares the mechanism that owns tiering" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0018-reachability-coherent.md">
- A skill's description is its tier-1 surface: name there every occasion the skill serves, with the context that makes it fire, and nothing else. Write every rule at the tier its occasion reads, and no higher: what sits at tier 1 is paid for by every session.
</straw-dog>

<installed by="ticket">
**P9** The first time a record or a reply names a ticket, name it by a link to its record whose text
carries its slug — the id may lead it; later mentions may be the id alone. Name one that has no
record yet by a slug and its state word.
</installed>

## Core and instance

`docs/` is substituted whole in a harness instance: a recipient project replaces its contents with
its own.

What core may not do is **depend** on it. Nothing under `.agents/` may reference a file in `docs/`,
or rely on one for its instruction or for any separable part of its own functioning. A core file
may name a path under `docs/` only when that path is a record a mechanism declares — the directory
that holds a kind of record, or a file that is one — never a particular record inside such a
directory: `docs/tickets/` and `docs/glossary.md` are painted doors; one particular ticket inside
`docs/tickets/` is a document only this project has. Content inside the
[local block](#project-local) is the instance's, not core's. A `<straw-dog>` exempts
nothing: its wrapper is stripped on install and whatever it wrapped ships. Core names a ticket
only in a straw dog's binding — never in a link, never as a bare id in prose — since a recipient
can resolve neither.

## Document load-bearing, code&comment the rest

A project's architecture, ADRs and glossary are the home for:
- Constitution — identity semantics, consistency model, source-of-truth rules
- Structure — service boundaries, data ownership, event/data flows, extension seams
- Load-bearing — see the definition below

A decision forms in its owning ticket and lands in one of these when it is ready. A decision about a
mechanism lands in that mechanism's doc, and what was refuted in its evidence.

<straw-dog until="01-0012 is done" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0012-hierarchy-coherent.md">
Bad architectural documentation:
- Forecasts are stored in MongoDB collection forecast_hourly.

Better:
- Historical forecast issues must remain independently addressable by (location, valid_time, issue_time) because validation compares what was known at different issue times.
</straw-dog>

## What makes a thing "load-bearing"

- A decision or invariant whose violation would cause multiple parts of the system to become wrong, not merely require local refactoring.
- A thing is load-bearing when several of these are true: has high blast radius, crosses boundaries (i.e. services, persistence, APIs, ownership), other decisions depend on it, it protects an invariant,
is expensive to reverse, holds non-obvious rationale, long-standing.

- Counter-test: if it can be changed locally without understanding the rest of the architecture, it is not load-bearing.

## The loop

Two rings, joined at /align.

    session:   wake with /recall → /align → /conclude → (next session)
    delivery:  /ticket → /plan → /implement → /verify → /maintain → /ticket

/align opens the delivery ring and is where it returns whenever a decision is needed:
/spec for load-bearing shapes, /plan when the governing docs contradict, /verify when a finding needs one, /maintain when maintenance surfaces one. /ticket⇄/plan and /implement⇄/verify iterate as pairs.

Human checkpoints: every decision at /align; spec accepted; breakdown approved; commit; push;
next cycle at /maintain → /ticket.

Do not reopen an accepted decision without new evidence.

### Helpers

- /impact determines the scope and load-bearingness of the shape. Use it to evaluate work volume and its ticketing shape (spec for load-bearing work, tickets for mechanical), work units slicing or whether a shape deserves further investigation due to hidden complexity.
- /discover to investigate hidden complexity, by detecting what else the shape is.
- /dream is an experimental second "lobe" of the harness, aiming to reassess load-bearingness. It is optional, runs after /conclude, and writes dreams that /maintain and /align may pick up; it never amends rules.

## Self-improvement

<straw-dog until="01-0019 is done" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0019-harness-amends-itself-by-explicit-meta-rules.md">
- The rule was present and did not fire - usually means the rule was phrased wrong. This is a call for registration and rephrasing it - write rule failure to docs/rule-failures.md (or strike if exists) and suggests way to amend the rule to capture (use /mechanism and /skill-up for ideas)
- Keeping the register: an entry names the rules that were in play and proposes the amendment; a repeat strikes the entry it repeats rather than opening a second; an entry closes when its amendment lands, or is refused with its reason. Nothing here authorises deleting a rule.
</straw-dog>

## Autonomy

The project sets each switch in its local block, under *Project-local*; skills defer to those values.

| Switch | Meaning |
|---|---|
| commit | `ask`: commit only on explicit permission, per change. `auto`: commit when the work is verified. |
| push | `ask`: separate from commit, per push. `never`, `auto`. |
| next-cycle | `ask`: starting the next ticket after one lands needs a nod. `auto`. |
| breakdown | `ask`: a /ticket split needs approval before minting. `auto`. |
| repair | `report`: a clear violation of an explicit rule inside authorized work is fixed and reported. `ask`: show it first. |

`repair=report` holds only when all four are true: the governing rule is explicit, and cited; the
repair restores compliance inside the authorized work and keeps every other agreed contract; the
affected behaviour is understood well enough to say so; the result is verifiable against the
rule. Otherwise `/align`. *(the user, 2026-09-05)*

## Project-local

<installed by="mechanism-shape">
**R7** A project's own answers and overrides are authored in one file beside the entry file,
`local.rules.md`, in the rules-file format, and reach a file only as the local block — the
installed block whose owner is `local` — which the installer writes after every mechanism's block
there, so the project's answer is what a reader meets after core's rule. An override names the rule it
overrides. A local change to a rule is written in the local file, never into a skill or the entry
file: `inject_rules.py --check` fails on a block that differs from its source and on a block
nothing owns, and the repair is the local file, re-installed. The local block is the project's,
not core's, and a redeploy preserves it.
</installed>

<installed by="local">
**L1** This repository develops the shared dev harness using its own loop; its own architecture and
progress live in docs/ like any other project's — the instance half doing its job, not a leak.
Terms: docs/glossary.md, this project's own; the method's are .agents/glossary.md's. What each
version of the entry contract changed: docs/research/entry-contract-findings.md.

**L2** commit=ask · push=ask · next-cycle=ask · breakdown=ask · repair=report
</installed>

## Straw dogs

Wrap anything a live ticket will change, as you write it — or, for text already written, in the
pass that mints the ticket or decides that it will change it:
`<straw-dog until="condition" ticket="path">`, or in code a `TODO` naming the ticket. Treat *not
yet*, *until*, *once it exists*, *for now*, *untested* in your own text as the same signal: find
the ticket, or mint one. Wrap at the authored home, never where the harness installs or derives it.
Make the condition testable and the ticket path repository-relative. Write the body to stand on
its own: it is what a recipient receives once the wrapper is stripped, so it reads whole without
the condition and names no ticket — the binding does. Leave what no ticket would change
unwrapped.

Follow a straw dog like any other rule until its condition is visibly met; then act on reality,
report the stale block, and do not treat the contradiction as a violation.

# Memory

- [Edit with edit tools, not scripts](edit-with-edit-tools-not-scripts.md) — a script's diff is invisible in the transcript; the user reads changes as they happen.
- [Write for a capable model](write-for-a-capable-model.md) — I pad rules with the definition, the example and the implication; all three get cut.
- [Problem before machinery](problem-before-machinery.md) — open an align with the concrete failures and the user's own prior words; a coined term or a design question first loses them.
- [Fix the cause, not just the register](fix-the-cause-not-just-the-register.md) — a rule failure entry ending in "not landed" ends the turn short; find the decisive fact and land the amendment in the same pass.
- [Deliver rules through the installer](deliver-rules-through-the-installer.md) — a mechanism's rule lands as an installed block into every occasion that reads it, never as hand-written prose; "otherwise you make it tier 3".

<pasted_content id="0730">
https://github.com/dveyarangi/goodwolf-harness - your review, please
I read the README and AGENTS.md; I haven't opened the skills, the scripts or their tests yet, so this is a review of the design and its entry surface, not the implementation.
Great
Records as the authority, sessions as history. The rule that session notes never decide what is still open is the most important idea here. It is also the one most homegrown agent setups get wrong: they pile up chat summaries and let the newest one win.
One home per rule, enforced by a check. Installed blocks with an owner, plus `inject_rules.py --check` failing on drift or on an orphan block, turns "keep instructions consistent" from a hope into a test. Most prompt-engineering setups have nothing like it.
The rule-failure register. Treating a rule that didn't fire as a phrasing bug, logging which rules were in play, and striking repeats instead of duplicating them is a postmortem culture aimed at the instructions rather than the code. The closing condition (the amendment lands, or it is refused with a reason) keeps the register from turning into a graveyard.
Straw dogs. Your stated limitations are themselves bound to tickets and stripped on install, so the "Not yet" list is tracked debt, not marketing hedging. Treating "for now", "until" and "untested" in the agent's own text as a trigger is a nice touch.
The load-bearing definition. The counter-test ("if it can be changed locally without understanding the rest, it isn't") plus the MongoDB-collection versus issue-time-invariant example teaches the distinction better than the list of criteria does.
Falsifiable adoption criteria. The three things to watch over a few weeks are observable outcomes, which almost no methodology README offers.
Good enough
Autonomy switches. The idea is right, and the four conditions on `repair=report` are well drawn. The README shows each switch as `ask`/`auto`, but the AGENTS.md table gives push a `never` option too, so the README undersells it.
Install safety. Refusing to overwrite, writing nothing on refusal, and handling Windows symlinks explicitly are all solid. How much can be done without tooling, via instructions, is honestly scoped.
Core/instance separation. The "painted doors" rule is precise. It will need a worked example the first time a recipient trips over it.
Missing
Enforcement at the host. You list it as a known gap, but I'd rank it first. The whole method rests on compliance, and the rule-failure register only works after something has already gone wrong. Claude Code hooks, and their equivalents in the other hosts, could hard-block `git commit` and `git push` when the switch is `ask`. That is cheap to build and turns your two highest-stakes rules from trusted into enforced.
A light path for small work. Also acknowledged, but it is the biggest adoption risk. If a one-line fix has to go through ticket, plan, implement, verify and maintain, people will route around the harness, and routing around it quietly breaks the records' authority. Even a declared "chore" path (ticket plus verify, no plan) would help.
Context budget. You state the tier-1 cost principle, but there's no number. AGENTS.md is about 9.5 KB before `/recall` reads anything, and recall's reading grows with the project. It would help to measure tokens spent before the first useful action and track that per version of the entry contract.
Instrumentation for the three outcomes. "Watch whether an agent re-decides less" is right, but nothing records it. `/conclude` could log reopened decisions and rebuilt context, so the evaluation comes out of the records instead of someone's impression.
Recall when the records are wrong. `/maintain` repairs drift, but `/recall` runs first and trusts the records. What should the agent do when a record contradicts the code it is looking at? That needs an explicit precedence rule.
Redundant
`/dream` sits in the entry file. It is experimental and optional, yet every session pays for it at tier 1, which breaks your own "no higher than its occasion" rule. It belongs in its skill's description only.
`.obsidian/` is committed. That's personal tooling state in a repo other people will clone.
`dev-skills.png` and `dev-skills-readme.png` both sit at the root next to the `.excalidraw` source. One image is probably enough.
Contradictory
Occam versus the surface area. "Fewest parts, remove before you add" sits beside two rings, around ten skills, three helpers, mechanisms, straw dogs, a coined term (shape) and a dream lobe. Each piece may be justified, but the README never makes that argument. A newcomer sees the parts count and not the reasoning behind it.
"Do not generalize from one shape" versus a method developed with itself. The harness's main proving ground is itself. By its own first rule, the general method should wait until a second, materially different project forces the same concepts. If you have that second project (the forecast example suggests your weather work), the README should say so. It's the strongest evidence you could offer.
Self-improvement versus "improvements stay in that project." The learning loop is local, so a rule-failure fix in one instance never reaches core. It's listed under "Not yet", but as written the headline claim of self-improvement is per-instance only.
Precision in the tier-1 file. The Self-improvement section is the least carefully written text in the file ("write rule failure to … and suggests way to amend"). The rule IDs are also used inconsistently: P9, R7, L1 and L2 are labeled, while most rules have no ID. For a file whose premise is that wording decides whether a rule fires, that section deserves the same care as the Straw dogs one.
README voice. The prose is dense and uses the method's own vocabulary before defining it, even though the README says the vocabulary is the agent's equipment, not the user's curriculum. The "How it works" paragraph would read better as the diagram plus three sentences.
Want me to go into the skills and scripts next? The `/mechanism` declaration check and `inject_rules.py` are where I'd most like to see whether the implementation holds up to the design.
not good enough. i need you to investigate the project
I cloned the repo and worked through it properly this time. I ran the full test suite, both as root and as an unprivileged user, and ran all four checks from the project's verification set. I installed the harness into a fresh git project, tried installing it over an existing `CLAUDE.md`, and ran an update. I tampered with an installed file to see whether `--check` catches it. I measured the context surfaces, traced which skills actually read each autonomy switch, and read the key skills, the mechanism declarations, the rule-failure register, the concerns file and all six runs of the adoption panel.
The findings I rank highest are the ones the project's own panels and register haven't caught.
Great
The install is solid, and I confirmed it. On a fresh repo it wrote 68 files, made both loader links and ran its three gates, finishing `arrived: true`. None of the origin's own local block (L1/L2) leaked into the recipient, and every straw-dog wrapper was stripped. When I edited one sentence of the installed `AGENTS.md`, `--check` exited 1 and named the file. Installing over an existing `CLAUDE.md` refused and wrote nothing, as documented.
The scripts are real engineering. About 3,900 lines of standard-library Python, 342 tests, 18 seconds. The failure contracts are tested, including partial writes, junctions that escape the tree and refusals that must write nothing.
The rule-failure register actually closes its loop. It has 11 entries, and each names the rules in play, why the rule didn't fire, the amendment, and a concrete grading event. Entry 3 was struck twice, and each strike records a new cause. I've rarely seen a self-improvement mechanism with this much evidence that it works.
Straw dogs are enforced, not just a convention. `mechanisms.py` treats an unbound "not yet" as a diagnostic, and the TODOs in the code name their tickets. The debt really is tracked.
The context cost at session start is modest. Skill descriptions total about 1.1k tokens and the entry file about 2.4k. My first review worried about the always-loaded context, and that worry was wrong (see the correction at the end).
Good enough
The commit discipline holds. All 168 commits use the step prefixes, so the history can be read by step (IMPLEMENT 28, ALIGN 22, MAINTAIN 21, and so on).
Session records stay bounded at about 800 to 1,100 words each. What grows is elsewhere; see below.
The glossary is sound but heavy. At 2,000 words and about 50 terms, it is effectively required reading, which the panel also flagged.
Contradictory
1. The commit permission has three homes, and they disagree. This is the highest-stakes rule in the harness, and it breaks the project's flagship principle of one home per rule:

* `AGENTS.md` defines `commit=auto` as "commit when the work is verified."
* `/implement` reads the switch correctly.
* `/commit`, the skill that actually commits, says in both its description and its body: never commit without explicit instruction or permission from the user, and do not push without explicit permission.

With `commit=auto`, the two skills contradict each other. The drift check can't catch this, because `/commit` is `Mechanism: not yet`, so its rule isn't an installed block.
2. Two of the five switches are read by nothing. Nothing reads `push` except the contradicting `/commit`. Nothing reads `next-cycle` except one line in the queue template. The only switches with real readers are `breakdown` (read by `/ticket`) and `repair` (read by `/verify`).
3. A fresh install has no switches at all. The installed `AGENTS.md` has no local block until someone writes `local.rules.md`. Skills told to "read `commit` from AGENTS.md" find nothing there, and no default is stated. In the first session of every recipient, the commit behaviour is undefined.
4. The README still claims an arrival flow that doesn't exist. Under "Works today," the README says the installing agent reads the moved-aside `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md`, skills and documents and works out at `/align` where each belongs. The harness skill contains no such instruction; it lists refusals only. Ticket `.0150`, which would build this, is still Planned. The latest commit is titled "stops claiming an unbacked install," but this claim survived it. Its straw dog says "arrival is guided by instructions," but the instructions don't exist.
5. "The links are never committed" holds only in the origin repo. The `.gitignore` entries for `.claude/skills` and `.cursor/skills` live in the harness repo, which doesn't ship them. In my test recipient, both links showed up as untracked, so the first `git add -A` commits them. That is exactly the Windows failure the panel's Cursor reader hit.
6. Update says everything changed. A no-op `--update` on an unchanged tree lists all 68 files as `written`. That goes beyond "updates don't say what changed": the report actively says everything did.
Missing
CI, and a green suite on Linux or macOS. The suite fails on POSIX. `test_refusals` cleans up its symlink with `link.rmdir()`, which is Windows-only behaviour; the production code (`_remove_link`) handles this correctly, but the test doesn't. `test_inject_rules` also assumes that `chmod` read-only stops a write, which fails under root, and root is the usual user in CI containers. There is no `.github/`, so the suite has evidently only ever been run on Windows, while the README claims three hosts and standard-library portability.
Honest check coverage. The README says the same checks hold your skills as hold the shipped ones. Measured, 20 of 23 skills carry `Mechanism: not yet`, and the "declared records" rule for `docs/` is a hand-maintained allowlist of 17 paths in `mechanisms.py` (honestly TODO'd). Today the checks hold three skills.
Tier-1 descriptions that meet the harness's own rule. The rule says a description names every occasion the skill serves, with the context that makes it fire. Four skills fall short:

* `celebrate`: "Use when it is time to celebrate something"
* `implement`: "Implement the agreed work into code"
* `improve-comments`: "Write or improve codebase comments"
* `conclude`, whose description has a typo ("curent") in text loaded every session.

Redundant, and out of balance
Records versus product. The repo holds about 210k words of process records (tickets 76k, RFCs 51k, research 45k, specs 14k) against about 3,900 lines of shipped code. The open parent ticket alone is 11k words, roughly 15k tokens, and it is exactly what `/recall` follows when it traces "the item in flight." That, not the entry file, is where session cost lives, and ticket `.0168` should measure it first.
Polishing the page instead of the product. The adoption panel ran six times on 26 September, and the verdicts never moved: one no and four not-yet, then five "not for my case." Every run names the same blockers: a light path for small work, the single-steerer limit, and taking over existing instructions. Between runs, 8 of the day's 18 commits are front-page FIXes. The page has probably reached diminishing returns, and the next panel run is only worth doing after `.0150`, the pacer's light path or `.0017.0020` lands.
Smaller items. `.obsidian/` is committed, `docs/research/audit-2026-09-05/` holds 1.5 MB of diffs and JSON, and there are three copies of the diagram. None of them ship, but they add weight to every clone.
What I'd do first

1. Move commit and push permission into one installed rule that `/commit` and `/implement` both receive. Either wire `next-cycle` and `push` to real readers or drop them. Ship defaults (all `ask`) in core so a fresh install is never undefined.
2. Make the harness add the loader links to the recipient's `.gitignore`, or to `.git/info/exclude`.
3. Fix the two POSIX test bugs and add a matrix CI across Windows, Linux and macOS.
4. Remove or straw-dog the README's arrival claim until `.0150` lands.
5. Make `--update` diff before it writes, so the report says what actually changed.

What changed from my first pass

* Withdrawn: that the entry file's context cost was a concern. Measured, it's small; the real cost is `/recall` following large tickets.
* Withdrawn: that `docs/rule-failures.md` in `AGENTS.md` might breach the rule about core citing instance files. It's an allowlisted path.
* Withdrawn: that the register was untested. It has struck entries with recorded grades.
* New: everything under Contradictory, the POSIX test failures and missing CI, the allowlist-based check coverage, the no-op update report, and the page-versus-product imbalance.
* Kept: the missing light path and the missing host enforcement. Both are already tracked in the project's own tickets.

This time I'm judging what the project is trying to do, not how far it has got. I took the goals from three places: the README's opening, the outcome of the parent ticket `01-0010`, and the principles in `AGENTS.md`. Read together, they contain three goals, not one, and most of my judgement is about how those three relate.

1. Memory. A disposable agent workforce gets institutional memory in the repository. Records, not chats, are the authority on what was decided, what is open and what was verified.
2. Distribution. Projects share one canonical method, contribute improvements back to it, and receive accepted changes mechanically, keeping their local behaviour, across three hosts. This is the outcome of `01-0010`.
3. Learning. The method improves itself: a rule that failed to fire is treated as a wording defect, recorded, reworded and graded.

Great
The memory goal diagnoses the problem correctly. Most tools in this space treat agent amnesia as a recall problem and add more context, memory stores or summaries. This goal treats it as a problem of authority: which record decides what is true now. "Session notes are history, never the authority" is the insight, and it is what separates this from memory plugins. It also targets the costliest failure in practice: an agent confidently re-deciding something settled, not an agent that merely forgets.
The goal can be proven wrong. The three signals are specific enough to fail: fewer re-decisions, work surviving the end of a session, and drift falling rather than documents piling up. Most methodologies state goals that can't be tested at all.
The learning goal is the most original of the three. Treating instructions as code that has bugs, with postmortems and regression grades, is a real idea. I don't know of a peer that aims at it.
Good enough
"Check instead of trust" is the right goal, stated at half strength. The README says the next agent, or you, can check the work instead of trusting it. As written, that goal is met by records an agent writes and checks an agent runs. A goal of verifiability should say what does the verifying that isn't also an agent. Hooks, CI and host enforcement belong in the goal itself, not in a "not yet" list. Without them, the goal is legibility, which is worth having but is a smaller claim.
Portability across three hosts is reasonable but costly for what it buys. It serves the distribution goal. The memory goal doesn't need it, and it multiplies the constraints behind every design decision.
Contradictory
Institutional memory versus a single steerer. An institution is several people by definition. A memory kept by one person steering agents is personal memory with good filing. The README lists the team limit as a temporary gap, but it is really an unanswered question about the goal: is this memory for a person's projects or for a team's? The two lead to different designs. A personal version can keep tickets as markdown in the repository with a private vocabulary. A team version has to live alongside the team's tracker, merge across branches, and be readable by people who never ran `/align`. The panel's verdict never moved in six runs because this question was never decided, not because any wording on the page was off.
Observability versus an agent dialect. The README says what you gain is observability, and also that the vocabulary and records are the agent's equipment, which you read only when you choose to. Observability only has value if a human reads the records when it matters, and at speed. Records written in the method's own vocabulary ("shape," "painted door," "straw dog," "wake") serve the agent reading them and cost the human auditing them. If the goal is observability, the human reader has to be the primary audience of the records. If the goal is agent continuity, observability is a side benefit and shouldn't be the headline.
Distribution presumes a population that doesn't exist. The distribution goal (contribute improvements upstream, receive accepted changes mechanically) is what a platform needs once it has many users. It was adopted on day one, with one author. It is also where most of the design weight comes from: the core/instance split, installed blocks and the injector, the stripping of straw-dog wrappers, mechanism declarations and the painted-door rule. That machinery answers "how do many projects share a method," a question the memory goal never asks. The entry file's first rule is not to generalise from one shape, and this goal generalises from projects that don't exist yet.
Proving it on itself is the most favourable test there is. "Developed with itself" is offered as validation, but the harness is a project whose product is mostly documents and rules, which is exactly what the method is best at. The goal needs its evidence from a project where the load-bearing work is code, deadlines and debugging, because that is where ceremony has the most to lose.
Missing
A cost term. None of the three goals says what the memory may cost. Institutional memory survives only while keeping it true is cheaper than ignoring it. Past that point people route around it, and a record that is routed around loses its authority, which is the thing the memory goal depends on. The goal needs a ceiling, for example: records stay proportional to the change, and a one-line fix leaves a one-line trace. Without one, the method has nothing that argues against its own growth. Here that growth is about 210k words of records against 4k lines of product.
What the memory is for, at the end. Fewer re-decisions and resumable work are intermediate outcomes. The final outcome should be named, whether that's shipping faster, shipping more correctly, or being able to hand work off. The choice matters, because it decides which ceremony earns its place: a project optimising for correctness keeps `/verify` heavy, while one optimising for throughput trims `/plan`.
The order of the goals. Nothing says which goal wins when they conflict, and they do conflict. Distribution wants a stable, general core, while learning wants the rules to keep changing. Memory wants low friction, and distribution adds machinery.
Redundant
Distribution, as a present goal. I'd move it from goal to option. Memory is the product and learning is the research. Distribution is what you do once a second and third author exist and ask for it. Until then, a clone plus a local rules file covers the need.
Verdict
The memory goal is correct and sharply framed, and the field around it underserves it. The learning goal is the most original part and should be named as research, so its cost isn't charged to users. The distribution goal is premature, and it is what makes the whole thing look heavy to people evaluating it.
Two decisions would clarify everything downstream: whether the memory is personal or institutional, and what the memory may cost. Settle those, and most of the current open tickets either become obvious or fall away.

Whether a host reads the link is not observable from inside a tree; the first session announcing

## Refusals, and what to do

Every refusal writes nothing and names its step.

- **A link the platform refused to create** is not a refusal: everything else landed, and the
  report's `pending` lines are the exact commands. Present them to the person verbatim, to run
  once in an elevated prompt, then run `--check`.
- **A `<project-local>` block in the entry file**: its content is the project's and the file is
  overwritten. Move each fact into `local.rules.md` as a rule, delete the block, run again.
- **A core file that differs from the announced ref**: an edit made in core. Keep it out of core
  — a project's answer or override goes in the local file — and run `--update --overwrite`,
  which replaces the file and names it.
- **A tree that announces no ref**: a copy that predates this script. `--update --overwrite` is
  required; nothing is deleted, and files under `.agents/` outside the manifest are reported as
  the project's own.
- **The injector refused**: an override naming a rule this ref no longer sends there, or a local
  anchor a new anchor now follows. Fix the local file, run `inject_rules.py local --install`, then
  `--check`.
- **A junction, a directory or a file where a link goes**: the project's own. Move it; a symlink
  goes there.
- **No readable `Repository:` line beside the script**: with no `--from`, the script cannot tell
  where core comes from. Pass `--from` this once, then restore the line — it is what every later
  run reads.
- **A ref whose harness skill carries no such line**: not the harness, in the same sense as an
  entry file with no announce line. Check the ref, or the repository.
- **The source itself as target**: the origin is never installed into.

## After the first install

The tree has core and no answers. Write `local.rules.md` beside the entry file, in the rules-file
format the entry file's *Project-local* section describes, from the environment you stand in: the
project's facts for the entry file, its autonomy switches, and its verification set — its
typechecker, its tests, every command required of landed work, read off its own toolchain. Then
`inject_rules.py local --install`, and `--check`. A project that wants core re-checked on every
`/verify` names `harness.py . --check` in that set.

I checked the review's factual claims against today's tree, and nearly all of them hold. A few numbers are from before last session (342 tests is now 289, 11 register entries is now 12), and it calls `.0150` Planned when it's Ready with its RFC written. None of that changes a conclusion.

## I'd take these as they are: confirmed bugs, cheap to fix

1. **`/commit` contradicts `commit=auto`.** [commit/SKILL.md](.agents/skills/commit/SKILL.md) says "never commit without explicit instruction or permission", while `/implement` says to read the switch. `push` has no reader except that blanket rule. This breaks our own "one home per rule" on the highest-stakes rule, and the drift check can't see it because `/commit` is still `Mechanism: not yet`, with its straw dog bound to [01-0017 io-graph-coherent](docs/tickets/01-0017-io-graph-coherent.md). I'd fix it ahead of that chain, as one installed rule that both skills receive.
2. **Core states no default for the switches.** "default" appears nowhere in AGENTS.md. Between an install and the local file being written, a recipient's commit behaviour is undefined. Core should state that every switch is `ask` until the project answers.
3. **Recipients' loader links aren't ignored by Git.** `harness.py` never touches `.gitignore` or `.git/info/exclude`, so the first `git add -A` in a recipient commits the links. That is the Windows failure behind issue #1. It belongs in [01-0010.0172 a-first-install-says-what-stopped-it](docs/tickets/01-0010.0172-a-first-install-says-what-stopped-it.md). I'd use `.git/info/exclude`, since that's per clone like the links themselves.
4. **`--update` rewrites every file and reports them all as written.** `_write` writes the whole manifest unconditionally, so the report can't tell a no-op from a change.
5. **Two tests fail on POSIX, and there's no CI.** [test_refusals.py:123](.agents/scripts/gw/test/test_refusals.py:123) calls `link.rmdir`, and the tests' read-only `chmod` doesn't stop a root user from writing. Both fit [01-0011.0090 a-test-catches-what-its-name-promises](docs/tickets/01-0011.0090-a-test-catches-what-its-name-promises.md). A Windows + Linux Actions matrix would have caught both.
6. **README "Works today" claims an arrival flow that doesn't exist.** Lines 93–98 describe the agent reading your moved-aside `CLAUDE.md` and sorting it at `/align`. The harness skill says nothing of the kind, and [01-0010.0150 harness-meets-a-tree-with-a-method](docs/tickets/01-0010.0150-harness-meets-a-tree-with-a-method.md) hasn't landed. The FIX commit that "stops claiming an unbacked install" missed this one. It should be straw-dogged to `.0150`, and it probably deserves a rule-failure entry.
7. **Smaller things:**
   - the "curent" typo in `/conclude`'s description, loaded every session
   - the sloppy Self-improvement paragraph in AGENTS.md
   - `/dream` taking tier-1 space for an optional, experimental skill

## I'd take these, with a different weight or fix

- **The cost term.** The reviewer is right, and I'd rank it highest among the goal-level points. The parent ticket is 11.4k words, and `/recall` follows it. Records total about 215k words against about 32k words of shipped skills plus 3.9k lines of Python. The reviewer compares records to Python only, which undercounts the product, but even so the records are roughly 6× what ships. [01-0010.0168 the-harness-measures-what-it-costs-and-saves](docs/tickets/01-0010.0168-the-harness-measures-what-it-costs-and-saves.md) should measure this first.
- **A light path for small work.** Every panel run names it. It lives in [01-0020 pacer](docs/tickets/01-0020-pacer.md) ("making the loop's ceremony switchable"), behind four refactors. I'd pull it forward.
- **Host enforcement.** A Claude Code hook that refuses `git commit` while `commit=ask` is cheap. [01-0010.0125 the-host-blocks-what-a-rule-forbids](docs/tickets/01-0010.0125-the-host-blocks-what-a-rule-forbids.md) waits on the whole cross-host survey in [01-0010.0120 host-delivery-surfaces](docs/tickets/01-0010.0120-host-delivery-surfaces.md), which looks over-sequenced. I still rank it below item 1: enforcing a rule that has three homes would enforce the contradiction.
- **Stop polishing the front page.** The facts check out: six panel runs, verdicts unchanged. I'd skip the next run until `.0150` or the light path lands.
- **Check coverage.** "The same checks hold your skills" is true of about 4 of 23 skills. The README should say so.

## Where I disagree

- **"Distribution is premature; make it an option."** Two recipients exist. frost_map is stranded behind the releases chain, and issue #1 came from ai-game-1. The distribution machinery answers real failures, not projects that might exist someday.
- **"You generalised from one shape / proved it only on itself."** The second shapes are those two recipients, and ai-game-1 is a code project. The fair criticism is that the evidence is thin and the README never mentions it, and I'd take that part.
- **"Recall trusts the records over the code."** `/recall` already says to cite the code where the code settled a question, and to report drift rather than fix it. A general precedence rule is still missing, but the gap is smaller than the review makes it sound.
- **`.obsidian/` and the three diagram copies.** Only you know whether the Obsidian config is deliberate: `.gitignore` already excludes its workspace file, which suggests it is. It's your call, not a finding.

## Two decisions that are yours, for `/align`

- **Personal or team memory?** The single-steerer limit may be why the panel verdict never moved. I don't think it can be settled from the records.
- **What the method is ultimately for** (shipping faster, shipping correctly, handing work off), **and what it may cost.** This decides which ceremony earns its place, and it feeds both `.0168` and the pacer's light path.

I agree with the reviewer's own correction at the end. It's four layers (memory, judgment, governance, self-correction), and the front page leads with the least distinctive one. But that's front-page work, and I'd put it after the bugs above.

**Suggested next step:** mint a small slice for items 1–2 (the commit/push rule and core defaults), fold items 3 and 5 into `.0172` and `.0090`, and straw-dog the README claim now. `breakdown=ask`, so I'll wait for your nod on the minting.

# Entry contract evidence

Evidence and evolution record for the entry contract — the versioned instructions every host
supplies at session start, announced verbatim by the session's first reply. The contract itself is
[AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md); this record holds what changed at each version and why, so a session
announcing a version can find out what it announced.

The version covers the **core** part only: the announce line, the general rules, the loop, the
switch roster with its meanings, and the `<straw-dog>` convention — `<temporary>` until v5.
The local block's values change without a bump.

**A recipient's line is not a version.** Since 2026-09-21 the harness mechanism stamps a
recipient's announce line `<repository>@<ref>, <date>` — the tag where the commit has one, the
short commit otherwise — so a recipient announces which core it holds and the check reads it
back. The hand-bumped version is the origin's, whose entry file cannot carry its own commit, and
this record keeps recording what each bump changed.

## v16 — 2026-09-21

**One core change:** the ticket mechanism's P9, the first block a mechanism installs into the
general rules — *name a ticket by a link to its record; one that has no record yet, by a slug
and its state word*. Decided by the user at
[01-0010.0150](../tickets/01-0010.0150-harness-meets-a-tree-with-a-method.md)'s `/plan`, after
a reply had named two tickets by ids like `.0145` before either existed. Tier 1 because the
occasion — naming a ticket in a reply — is every session's; installed from
`ticket.rules.md` rather than written by hand, so the tiering rule's owner and the injector both
see it.

## v15 — 2026-09-21

**One core change:** the tiering rule, in the general rules, wrapped on
[01-0018](../tickets/01-0018-reachability-coherent.md) under R5 until that ticket declares the
mechanism that owns it — *a skill's description is its tier-1 surface: name there every occasion
the skill serves, with the context that makes it fire, and nothing else; write every rule at the
tier its occasion reads, and no higher: what sits at tier 1 is paid for by every session*.
Decided by the user the evening [01-0010.0130](../tickets/done/01-0010.0130-harness-installs-into-another-tree.md)
closed, on three questions answered no from the tree: no maintenance pass holds skills to
`/skill-up`'s rules, `/skill-up` did not know the description is the whole of a skill's tier-1
presence, and the tier definitions had no owner. It is a meta-rule about how rules are written,
which is what the entry file holds, and every occasion that writes a rule reads it there.

1	# GoodWolf Harness
2	
3	Coding agents are capable engineers who forget everything when the session ends — and a different
4	one arrives next time. The harness gives that workforce an institutional memory in the repository:
5	what was decided and why, what is unfinished, what was verified and against what. Each session
6	reconstructs where the project stands from those records, not from a chat that is gone.
7	
8	The harness is yours to change. Your project's own rules — its test commands, whether the agent may
9	commit without asking — go in one local file that every install and update applies last; to change
10	a shipped rule, you override it there by name. You can add skills of your own: `/mechanism`, the
11	skill for declaring one, walks you through it, and the same checks then hold your skill as hold the
12	shipped ones. And when a rule was in place but the agent didn't follow it, the case is written down
13	and the rule reworded — a postmortem aimed at the instructions instead of the code.
14	
15	## How it works
16	
17	A session starts with `/recall`, which reads the project's records and finds where the work
18	stopped. `/align` settles with you whatever needs deciding, and the work picks up from there — one
19	step or several, through as many pieces of work as the session holds — until `/conclude` writes
20	down what the next session needs. A piece of work moves `/ticket` → `/plan` → `/implement` →
21	`/verify` → `/maintain`: it becomes a ticket with checkable acceptance criteria, gets a written
22	plan, is built test-first where it can be, and is verified against its ticket, its plan and the
23	project's own checks. Large work starts as a spec, aligned with you, and is split by `/ticket` into
24	thin slices that each go round the loop; `/impact` checks what each slice touches before it is cut.
25	Whenever a step needs a decision, it goes back to `/align`. `/verify` checks
26	the change; `/maintain` keeps the system of knowledge — a separate step for drift, checking that the
27	repository's documents still agree with each other and with the code, and repairing what doesn't.
28	
29	![The session ring — /recall, /align, /conclude — joined at /align to the delivery ring — /ticket, /plan, /implement, /verify, /maintain — around the project's records: tickets, RFCs, architecture, the codebase](dev-skills-readme.png)
30	
31	Decisions live in the architecture, ADRs and glossary; open work lives in tickets; session records
32	are history, never the authority on what is still open. What each record looks like is in its
33	format file: [tickets](.agents/skills/ticket/TICKET-FORMAT.md),
34	[ADRs](.agents/skills/align/ADR-FORMAT.md), [architecture](.agents/skills/align/ARCH-FORMAT.md),
35	[glossary](.agents/skills/align/GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).
36	
37	Where a person has to say yes is a switch — commit, push, start the next piece of work, split work
38	into tickets — each `ask` or `auto`, and one more for whether a clear rule violation is fixed and
39	reported or shown to you first:

# GoodWolf Harness

Coding agents are capable engineers who forget everything when the session ends — and a different
one arrives next time. The harness gives that workforce an institutional memory in the repository:
what was decided and why, what is unfinished, what was verified and against what. Each session
reconstructs where the project stands from those records, not from a chat that is gone.

The harness is yours to change. Your project's own rules — its test commands, whether the agent may
commit without asking — go in one local file that every install and update applies last; to change
a shipped rule, you override it there by name. You can add skills of your own: `/mechanism`, the
skill for declaring one, walks you through it, and the same checks then hold your skill as hold the
shipped ones. And when a rule was in place but the agent didn't follow it, the case is written down
and the rule reworded — a postmortem aimed at the instructions instead of the code.

## How it works

A session starts with `/recall`, which reads the project's records and finds where the work
stopped. `/align` settles with you whatever needs deciding, and the work picks up from there — one
step or several, through as many pieces of work as the session holds — until `/conclude` writes
down what the next session needs. A piece of work moves `/ticket` → `/plan` → `/implement` →
`/verify` → `/maintain`: it becomes a ticket with checkable acceptance criteria, gets a written
plan, is built test-first where it can be, and is verified against its ticket, its plan and the
project's own checks. Large work starts as a spec, aligned with you, and is split by `/ticket` into
thin slices that each go round the loop; `/impact` checks what each slice touches before it is cut.
Whenever a step needs a decision, it goes back to `/align`. `/verify` checks
the change; `/maintain` keeps the system of knowledge — a separate step for drift, checking that the
repository's documents still agree with each other and with the code, and repairing what doesn't.

![The session ring — /recall, /align, /conclude — joined at /align to the delivery ring — /ticket, /plan, /implement, /verify, /maintain — around the project's records: tickets, RFCs, architecture, the codebase](dev-skills-readme.png)

Decisions live in the architecture, ADRs and glossary; open work lives in tickets; session records
are history, never the authority on what is still open. What each record looks like is in its
format file: [tickets](.agents/skills/ticket/TICKET-FORMAT.md),
[ADRs](.agents/skills/align/ADR-FORMAT.md), [architecture](.agents/skills/align/ARCH-FORMAT.md),
[glossary](.agents/skills/align/GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).

Where a person has to say yes is a switch — commit, push, start the next piece of work, split work
into tickets — each `ask` or `auto`, and one more for whether a clear rule violation is fixed and
reported or shown to you first:

```
commit=ask · push=ask · next-cycle=ask · breakdown=ask · repair=report
```

**Why a loop.** Agents need keeping in check — most of all when one picks up where another
stopped. Each step has an agent say what it will do and leave a record of what it did, so work can
stop at any step and any agent can pick it up from the records, and the next agent, or you, can
check the work instead of trusting it. You don't run the steps: the skills hand the work on to each
other around the loop, so none needs calling by hand. The skills, the records and most of the
vocabulary are the agent's working equipment, not a curriculum: you meet a few terms when it asks
you to decide something, and the records when you choose to read them. What you gain is observability — what was
decided, planned and verified, there to read when it matters. Every stop for your say is optional:
a switch set to `auto` lets the loop run on, and `commit=auto` commits each piece of work once it
is verified.

Every session opens the same way: it names the version of the rules it runs and reads where the
work stands. A session you drive by hand and one started to take a chunk of work unattended begin
from the same place.

---
name: commit
description: >-
  Rules for committing changes to the code repository. Never commit without explicit instruction or permission from the user.
---

<straw-dog until="01-0017 declares the commit mechanism" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0017-io-graph-coherent.md">Mechanism: not yet</straw-dog>

- Commit the work in current session only. Do not commit changes of other session that might represent a work in progress. When in doubt, ask user.

- Look at pending changes; group them by content aligning with origin topic, ticket, rfc or change type (documentation, code, CI, skills).

- Separate implementation and documentation commits.

- Prefix the subject with the loop step that produced the work, uppercase, then a colon:
  `ALIGN`, `SPEC`, `TICKET`, `PLAN`, `IMPLEMENT`, `VERIFY`, `MAINTAIN`, `DISCOVER`, `RECALL`,
  `CONCLUDE`. Three sit outside the ring: `FIX` for a repair taken on its own, `EQUIP` for
  a change to the harness's own installation, and `DREAM` for a record the second lobe wrote. One
  prefix per commit — where the work spans two steps, take the dominant one and name the bleed in
  the message. The prefix says which step produced the work, never which files it touched: what
  changed is visible in the diff, and which step produced it is not.

- In case the file changes belong to several groups, commit the file with the group forming its dominant topic and mention the bleed in that commit's message.

- Do not reference sessions in commit comments, sessions are ephemeral.

- Unless already working in branch or instructed to branch - commit to default branch.

- When committing a code change, first run the checks the repository defines for itself — its
  linter, its formatter in check mode, its type checker, its tests. Pure doc changes need none
  of them. **Read them from where the project states them; never carry them here.** A commit
  skill holding a project's commands is a second home for them, and it is wrong for every
  project but the one it was written in.

- Do not commit without explicit instruction or permission from user.
- Separately, do not push without explicit instruction or permission from user.

class AnUpdate(TwoTrees):
    def setUp(self) -> None:
        super().setUp()
        self.run_harness("--install")
        self.write_target(
            "local.rules.md",
            "# local — this project's rules\n\n| target | anchor |\n|---|---|\n| `AGENTS.md` | `## Project-local` |\n\n"
            "## L1 — ours\n\n- **target** `AGENTS.md`\n- **authority** the user, 2026-09-21\n\n<rule>\nOur answer.\n</rule>\n",
        )
        self.local_before = (self.target / "local.rules.md").read_bytes()

    def write_target(self, name: str, text: str) -> None:
        path = self.target / name
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with path.open("w", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as handle:
            handle.write(text)

    def test_leaves_the_local_file_byte_identical_and_restores_its_block_last(self) -> None:
        self.write(KEEPER, "# Keeper\n\nKeep more things.\n")
        self.commit("core moved")

        status, report = self.run_harness("--update")

        self.assertEqual(self.local_before, (self.target / "local.rules.md").read_bytes())
        self.assertIn("Keep more things.", self.target_text(KEEPER))
        entry = self.target_text("AGENTS.md")
        self.assertIn('<installed by="local">\n**L1** Our answer.\n</installed>', entry)
        self.assertGreater(entry.index('<installed by="local">'), entry.index("## Project-local"))
        self.assertIn(f"@{self.short_head()}, ", entry)
        self.assertTrue(report["gates"]["ref"]["passed"], report["gates"]["ref"])
        self.assertTrue(report["gates"]["injector"]["passed"], report["gates"]["injector"])

    def test_deletes_what_left_the_manifest_and_the_directories_it_emptied_when_the_line_announces_a_ref(self) -> None:
        self.remove(".agents/glossary.md", ".agents/scripts/gw/test")
        self.commit("the glossary and the shipped tests leave")

        status, report = self.run_harness("--update")

        self.assertEqual(
            [".agents/glossary.md", ".agents/scripts/gw/test/test_arrival.py"], sorted(report["deleted"])
        )
        self.assertFalse((self.target / ".agents/glossary.md").exists())
        self.assertFalse((self.target / ".agents/scripts/gw/test").exists())

    def test_reports_the_recipients_own_files_under_core_and_leaves_them(self) -> None:
        self.write_target(".agents/skills/theirs/SKILL.md", "Mechanism: unowned by design — theirs\n\n# Theirs\n")

        status, report = self.run_harness("--update")

        self.assertEqual([".agents/skills/theirs/SKILL.md"], report["own"])
        self.assertTrue((self.target / ".agents/skills/theirs/SKILL.md").is_file())

    def test_with_no_announced_ref_overwrite_replaces_every_core_file_and_deletes_nothing(self) -> None:
        entry = self.target / "AGENTS.md"
        entry.write_text(entry.read_text(encoding="utf-8").replace(f"{self.source.name}@", "v"), encoding="utf-8")
        self.write_target(".agents/stale.md", "left over from a hand install\n")
        self.remove(".agents/glossary.md")
        self.commit("the glossary leaves")

        status, report = self.run_harness("--update", "--overwrite")

        self.assertEqual([], report["deleted"])
        self.assertTrue((self.target / ".agents/glossary.md").exists())
        self.assertIn(".agents/stale.md", report["own"])
        self.assertIn(f"@{self.short_head()}, ", self.target_text("AGENTS.md"))

    def test_overwrite_replaces_an_edited_core_file_and_names_it(self) -> None:
        (self.target / KEEPER).write_text("# Keeper, edited\n", encoding="utf-8")

        status, report = self.run_harness("--update", "--overwrite")

        self.assertEqual([KEEPER], report["replaced"])
        self.assertIn("Keep things.", self.target_text(KEEPER))

    def test_a_link_that_resolves_is_left_alone(self) -> None:
        if not platform_makes_symlinks():
            self.skipTest("this platform refuses to create a symlink; a kept link cannot be made")

        status, report = self.run_harness("--update")

        self.assertEqual(["kept", "kept"], [link["state"] for link in report["links"]])

    def test_an_injector_refusal_is_unfinished_and_names_the_resume(self) -> None:
        self.write_target(
            "local.rules.md",
            "# local\n\n| target | anchor |\n|---|---|\n| `AGENTS.md` | `## Project-local` |\n\n"
            "## L1 — ours\n\n- **target** `AGENTS.md`\n- **overrides** `sample/P9`\n"
            "- **authority** the user, 2026-09-21\n\n<rule>\nOur answer.\n</rule>\n",
        )

        status, report = self.run_harness("--update")

        self.assertEqual(1, status)
        self.assertIn("inject:", report["refusals"][0])
        self.assertIn("L1 overrides sample/P9", report["refusals"][0])
        self.assertIn("harness.py . --check", report["refusals"][0])
        self.assertIn("Keep things.", self.target_text(KEEPER))

RFC = "docs/rfc/01-0010.0040-install-plan.md"

class Refusal(RepositoryCase):
    def setUp(self) -> None:
        super().setUp()
        self.write(TICKET, "# Install /plan\n")
        self.write(RFC, "# Install /plan — plan\n")
        self.write("docs/tickets/README.md", "# Queue\n\n[plan](01-0010.0040-install-plan.md)\n")

    def refused_for(self, pairs: list[tuple[str, str]]) -> str:
        untouched = self.snapshot()

        self.assertEqual(untouched, self.snapshot(), "a refusal must not change a single byte")

    def test_a_record_that_is_not_there_cannot_move(self) -> None:

## General rules

A **shape** is whatever is under consideration, held between an idea and a thing: formed enough
to have a context and a structure, not yet exhausted by any one realization. Being a shape says
nothing about being load-bearing — an implementation method is a shape too. → [glossary](.agents/glossary.md).

- Do not generalize from one shape. Preserve a seam. Generalize only when a second materially different shape forces the same concept.
- Explore shape context - what is the shape one of? what are its relationships? does its scope overlap any other shape?
- Explore shape structure - how this shape is/can be built? does expanding its structure change the contract or even what the shape is?

- Changing how the work is done — a skill, a check, a record, the loop — is mechanism work: use [/mechanism](.agents/skills/mechanism/SKILL.md). Building what the project produces is not.

- An `<installed>` block in a file is not that file's to edit. Change the rule in the rules file of the mechanism named on the block, and re-install.

- Recency for evidence, longevity for principles.

- Clarity and simplicity first — Occam's razor: take the shape with the fewest parts that does the job, and remove before you add.

<straw-dog until="01-0018 declares the mechanism that owns tiering" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0018-reachability-coherent.md">
- A skill's description is its tier-1 surface: name there every occasion the skill serves, with the context that makes it fire, and nothing else. Write every rule at the tier its occasion reads, and no higher: what sits at tier 1 is paid for by every session.
</straw-dog>

<installed by="ticket">
**P9** The first time a record or a reply names a ticket, name it by a link to its record whose text
carries its slug — the id may lead it; later mentions may be the id alone. Name one that has no
record yet by a slug and its state word.
</installed>

## Core and instance

`docs/` is substituted whole in a harness instance: a recipient project replaces its contents with
its own.

What core may not do is **depend** on it. Nothing under `.agents/` may reference a file in `docs/`,
or rely on one for its instruction or for any separable part of its own functioning. A core file
may name a path under `docs/` only when that path is a record a mechanism declares — the directory
that holds a kind of record, or a file that is one — never a particular record inside such a
directory: `docs/tickets/` and `docs/glossary.md` are painted doors; one particular ticket inside
`docs/tickets/` is a document only this project has. Content inside the
[local block](#project-local) is the instance's, not core's. A `<straw-dog>` exempts
nothing: its wrapper is stripped on install and whatever it wrapped ships. Core names a ticket
only in a straw dog's binding — never in a link, never as a bare id in prose — since a recipient
can resolve neither.

## Document load-bearing, code&comment the rest

A project's architecture, ADRs and glossary are the home for:
- Constitution — identity semantics, consistency model, source-of-truth rules
- Structure — service boundaries, data ownership, event/data flows, extension seams
- Load-bearing — see the definition below

A decision forms in its owning ticket and lands in one of these when it is ready. A decision about a
mechanism lands in that mechanism's doc, and what was refuted in its evidence.

<straw-dog until="01-0012 is done" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0012-hierarchy-coherent.md">

- Forecasts are stored in MongoDB collection forecast_hourly.

Better:
- Historical forecast issues must remain independently addressable by (location, valid_time, issue_time) because validation compares what was known at different issue times.
</straw-dog>

## What makes a thing "load-bearing"

- A decision or invariant whose violation would cause multiple parts of the system to become wrong, not merely require local refactoring.
- A thing is load-bearing when several of these are true: has high blast radius, crosses boundaries (i.e. services, persistence, APIs, ownership), other decisions depend on it, it protects an invariant,
is expensive to reverse, holds non-obvious rationale, long-standing.

- Counter-test: if it can be changed locally without understanding the rest of the architecture, it is not load-bearing.

## The loop

Two rings, joined at /align.

    session:   wake with /recall → /align → /conclude → (next session)
    delivery:  /ticket → /plan → /implement → /verify → /maintain → /ticket

/align opens the delivery ring and is where it returns whenever a decision is needed:
/spec for load-bearing shapes, /plan when the governing docs contradict, /verify when a finding needs one, /maintain when maintenance surfaces one. /ticket⇄/plan and /implement⇄/verify iterate as pairs.

Human checkpoints: every decision at /align; spec accepted; breakdown approved; commit; push;
next cycle at /maintain → /ticket.

Do not reopen an accepted decision without new evidence.

### Helpers

- /impact determines the scope and load-bearingness of the shape. Use it to evaluate work volume and its ticketing shape (spec for load-bearing work, tickets for mechanical), work units slicing or whether a shape deserves further investigation due to hidden complexity.
- /discover to investigate hidden complexity, by detecting what else the shape is.
- /dream is an experimental second "lobe" of the harness, aiming to reassess load-bearingness. It is optional, runs after /conclude, and writes dreams that /maintain and /align may pick up; it never amends rules.

## Self-improvement

<straw-dog until="01-0019 is done" ticket="docs/tickets/01-0019-harness-amends-itself-by-explicit-meta-rules.md">
- The rule was present and did not fire - usually means the rule was phrased wrong. This is a call for registration and rephrasing it - write rule failure to docs/rule-failures.md (or strike if exists) and suggests way to amend the rule to capture (use /mechanism and /skill-up for ideas)
- Keeping the register: an entry names the rules that were in play and proposes the amendment; a repeat strikes the entry it repeats rather than opening a second; an entry closes when its amendment lands, or is refused with its reason. Nothing here authorises deleting a rule.
</straw-dog>

## Autonomy

The project sets each switch in its local block, under *Project-local*; skills defer to those values.

| Switch | Meaning |
|---|---|
| commit | `ask`: commit only on explicit permission, per change. `auto`: commit when the work is verified. |
| push | `ask`: separate from commit, per push. `never`, `auto`. |
| next-cycle | `ask`: starting the next ticket after one lands needs a nod. `auto`. |
| breakdown | `ask`: a /ticket split needs approval before minting. `auto`. |
| repair | `report`: a clear violation of an explicit rule inside authorized work is fixed and reported. `ask`: show it first. |

`repair=report` holds only when all four are true: the governing rule is explicit, and cited; the
repair restores compliance inside the authorized work and keeps every other agreed contract; the
affected behaviour is understood well enough to say so; the result is verifiable against the
rule. Otherwise `/align`. *(the user, 2026-09-05)*

## Project-local

<installed by="mechanism-shape">
**R7** A project's own answers and overrides are authored in one file beside the entry file,
`local.rules.md`, in the rules-file format, and reach a file only as the local block — the
installed block whose owner is `local` — which the installer writes after every mechanism's block
there, so the project's answer is what a reader meets after core's rule. An override names the rule it
overrides. A local change to a rule is written in the local file, never into a skill or the entry
file: `inject_rules.py --check` fails on a block that differs from its source and on a block
nothing owns, and the repair is the local file, re-installed. The local block is the project's,
not core's, and a redeploy preserves it.
</installed>

<installed by="local">
**L1** This repository develops the shared dev harness using its own loop; its own architecture and
progress live in docs/ like any other project's — the instance half doing its job, not a leak.
Terms: docs/glossary.md, this project's own; the method's are .agents/glossary.md's. What each
version of the entry contract changed: docs/research/entry-contract-findings.md.

**L2** commit=ask · push=ask · next-cycle=ask · breakdown=ask · repair=report
</installed>

## Straw dogs

Wrap anything a live ticket will change, as you write it — or, for text already written, in the
pass that mints the ticket or decides that it will change it:
`<straw-dog until="condition" ticket="path">`, or in code a `TODO` naming the ticket. Treat *not
yet*, *until*, *once it exists*, *for now*, *untested* in your own text as the same signal: find
the ticket, or mint one. Wrap at the authored home, never where the harness installs or derives it.
Make the condition testable and the ticket path repository-relative. Write the body to stand on
its own: it is what a recipient receives once the wrapper is stripped, so it reads whole without
the condition and names no ticket — the binding does. Leave what no ticket would change
unwrapped.

Follow a straw dog like any other rule until its condition is visibly met; then act on reality,
report the stale block, and do not treat the contradiction as a violation.

# Comment Guide for LLM-Generated Code

## Core Rule

Comments should explain **intent, constraints, and danger**.

They should not translate code into English.

A good comment answers questions the code cannot answer clearly by itself:

* Why does this exist?
* Why was this approach chosen?
* Why was an obvious alternative rejected?
* What domain rule is being enforced?
* What invariant must remain true?
* What external constraint shapes this code?
* What danger should future maintainers notice?

## First Prefer Clear Code

Before adding a comment, check whether the idea can be expressed better through:

* a clearer name
* a smaller function
* a stronger type
* a better module boundary
* a more explicit interface
* a simpler control flow

If the code can be clarified directly, improve the code instead of adding a comment.

## Good Comments Explain Why

Good comments explain reasoning, not mechanics.

```python
# We prefer freshness over provider priority here because stale severe-weather data is dangerous.
```

```python
# Invariant: all ranges in a Coverage share the same geometry.
```

```python
# Visual Crossing reports some hourly values in local time; normalize before merging.
```

## Bad Comments Repeat the Code

Avoid comments that simply narrate what the next line already says.

```python
# Increment i
i += 1
```

```python
# Loop over providers
for provider in providers:
    ...
```

```python
# Check if provider can answer the request
if provider.can_answer(selection):
    ...
```

These comments add noise without adding understanding.

## Comment Stable Knowledge

Prefer comments about things that are unlikely to change accidentally:

* domain rules
* invariants
* protocol contracts
* vendor quirks
* non-local consequences
* safety assumptions
* ordering requirements
* rejected design alternatives

Avoid comments that describe tiny implementation details likely to rot.

## Comment Where Wrong Assumptions Are Likely

Use comments when a future reader may make a plausible but wrong assumption.

```python
# Do not reorder these rules: later checks assume rain risk was already classified.
```

```python
# We do not cache raw vendor JSON here: cache readers need canonical Coverage semantics.
```

```python
# This module normalizes vendor weather semantics.
# It must not perform provider selection or fallback.
```

## Public API Comments

Public API comments should explain correct usage, expectations, and contract boundaries.

They should describe:

* what the caller may assume
* what the caller must provide
* what errors mean
* what is intentionally not guaranteed

Example:

```python
# Returns canonical Coverage in the provider's native geometry.
# If the selection specifies a lattice, the provider may homogenize onto that lattice.
```

## Internal Comments

Internal comments should explain why the implementation has this shape.

They are useful for:

* tricky domain logic
* external API weirdness
* performance-sensitive choices
* surprising ordering
* compatibility constraints
* intentionally ugly but necessary code

## TODO Comments

Always mark the temporary code, that will be dissolved/changed by some future work, with TODO (temporary) (and add reference to related doc/concern)

Keep the marker exact and put ownership after the colon, for example:
`TODO (temporary): [0117](path) replaces this shim.` Numeric IDs remain document references, not
part of the TODO syntax.

Other than that, TODO should name a concrete missing action.


Bad:
```python
# TODO: clean this horrible mess later
```

Good:
```python
# TODO: split provider normalization from HTTP retry policy.
```

Good TODOs should be actionable, specific, and easy to search.


## # @hotpath
Hotpath comment `# @hotpath` may appear at method or code block.
It means that this is important root flow of the program and deserves better comments inside. Do not delete comments inside hotpath blocks, but you can finetune or trim them when overexplaining.


## Avoid Comment Apologies

Do not use comments to excuse unclear code. Either make it clear, mark it with TODO or explain why the shape is chosen:

Bad:

```python
# Sorry, this is ugly but it works.
```

Better:

```python
# Provider returns mixed local/UTC timestamps; keep this branch until upstream fixes export format. Concern/doc ref ###
```

## Preferred Comment Targets

Prefer comments above:

* modules
* classes
* functions
* public APIs
* tricky blocks
* invariants
* dangerous assumptions

Avoid dense line-by-line comments, unless on hotpath and tell a story.

## Final Checklist

Before keeping a comment, ask:

1. Does it explain something the code cannot express clearly?
2. Will it still be true after small implementation changes?
3. Does it prevent a plausible future mistake?
4. Does it explain intent, constraint, or danger?
5. Is it more useful than improving the code itself?

If yes, keep it.

If not, remove it.

## Summary

Good comments preserve design intent.

Bad comments narrate syntax.

Write comments for the maintainer who understands the language, but does not yet understand the context.

If architecture entry/decision/description already exists, prefer link to docs instead elaborating on it.

## The align this ticket owns

- **The unit of work** the costs are counted against — a closed ticket, a commit, a session — so a
  long session and a short one compare.
- **Which human turns are burden.** An approval at a switch set to `ask`, a decision at `/align`,
  and a correction of the agent are different costs; only the last is pure burden, and the others
  are what the switches exist to trade.
- **The outcome proxies** for the three the review named, each from a record that already exists —
  corrections of the *we already decided* kind, the turns a session spends re-establishing where
  it stands, `/maintain`'s findings per pass and the straw-dog count over time.
- **What leaves the machine.** Transcripts are the person's and private; what is published is an
  aggregate, and where it lives — this repository's instance half, or the front page.
- **Which hosts** are counted, and whether the trend is this project's alone or every recipient's
  that opts in.
- **When it runs** — at `/conclude`, at a release, on request — and so who reads it.

## What to build

The align's decision landed in its durable home, and this ticket rewritten in place to the feature.

=====
## The align this ticket owns

- **Which hosts.** Each hooks differently, and some may not at all; what Codex and Cursor can
  refuse is unobserved, which is `.0120`'s to find out.
- **Which rules.** Only a rule whose breach is a visible action can be refused — the switches
  (`commit`, `push`) are the obvious cases; a rule about what the agent writes or decides is not.
- **Where the configuration lives.** A hook is configured in a host file a project often already
